note: A man betrothed a woman with a mat of myrtle branches. Onlookers told him it was not worth even a peruta, the smallest coin, so he said she should be betrothed with the four dinars wrapped inside it. She took the mat and said nothing. Rava ruled that this was silence after the money had already been given, and such silence is nothing: it does not show that she accepted.
why: The discussion has been listing improper ways of betrothing a woman; right after this case Rava shows where his rule comes from, a baraita about a coin first handed over as a deposit, and the Gemara works out that silence there does not count as consent.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who rules on the case

terms.meaning: The first, legally binding stage of Jewish marriage, made when a man gives a woman something of value for that purpose and she accepts it.
A silver coin, worth far more than a peruta.

note: Rav Ḥisda kept praising Rav Hamnuna to Rav Huna as a great man, and Rav Huna asked to have him sent over. When Rav Hamnuna came, Rav Huna saw that he did not cover his head with a cloth, as Torah scholars did, and asked why. Rav Hamnuna said it was because he was not married. Rav Huna turned his face away from him and said: See that you do not see my face until you marry.
why: The Gemara has just discussed whether a man should study Torah first or marry first; afterward it explains that Rav Huna acted on his own view that a man still unmarried at twenty spends all his days in thoughts of sin.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: A Sage who praises Rav Hamnuna to Rav Huna

people.name: Rav Hamnuna
people.about: A promising scholar who is not yet married

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: The senior Sage who rebukes Rav Hamnuna for not marrying

note: Rav Dimi, arriving in Babylonia from the Land of Israel, reported that Dama ben Netina was once wearing a fine cloak of gold and sitting among the nobles of Rome. His mother came, tore the garment off him, smacked him on the head and spat in his face, and he did not embarrass her.
why: The Gemara is showing how far the duty to honor parents goes, using Dama ben Netina, a gentile whose honor for his father earned him a great reward; Rav Dimi adds this second report of his restraint toward his mother.

people.name: Rav Dimi
people.about: A Sage who brings this report from the Land of Israel

people.name: Dama ben Netina
people.about: A gentile known for honoring his parents

note: In a Pumbedita butcher shop, a man from Neharde'a was told to wait until Rav Yehuda bar Yeḥezkel's servant was served, and mocked Rav Yehuda with an insulting name. Rav Yehuda excommunicated him and, told he often called people slaves, proclaimed him a slave. The man summoned Rav Yehuda to Rav Naḥman's court. There Rav Yehuda corrected Rav Naḥman's every word and offer, until Rav Naḥman's wife Yalta told him to get it over with. When the man claimed descent from the Hasmonean kings, Rav Yehuda quoted Shmuel that anyone who says so is a slave, and Rav Mattana, arriving that day, confirmed it. The man was proclaimed a slave and marriage contracts were torn up. When people chased Rav Yehuda to stone him, he threatened to reveal more, and they threw down their stones.
why: The Gemara has just taught that whoever calls others flawed is himself flawed, and Shmuel's saying that he disqualifies with his own flaw; Rav Yehuda cites that very teaching in court to justify declaring the man a slave.

people.name: Rav Yehuda bar Yeḥezkel
people.about: A Sage of Pumbedita, called Rav Yehuda, who excommunicates the man and is summoned to court

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: The judge in Neharde'a, son-in-law of the Exilarch, who hears the case

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: The Sage who advises Rav Yehuda to answer the summons

people.name: Yalta
people.about: Rav Naḥman's wife, who tells him to end the exchange

people.name: Rav Mattana
people.about: A Sage who arrives after thirteen years away and confirms Shmuel's ruling

terms.meaning: A ban imposed by the Sages that cuts a person off from normal dealings with the community until he repents.
The hereditary head of the Jewish community in Babylonia.
The Jewish royal dynasty of the Second Temple period; the story says only slaves remained of their line.
The ketubba, the document a husband gives his wife at marriage; tearing it up here marks a marriage found to be invalid.
